## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by
the person making the decision, reviewed by the team.

consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

# Dependency Management

Owner: Developer Experience (DevEx)

## Adding a dependency

Before adding a third-party dependency, check that the standard library or
an existing internal library does not already solve the problem. The pull
request that adds a dependency explains why it is needed, links to the
project's license, and notes its maintenance status (last release, open
issues, number of maintainers).

## Allowed licenses

Permissive licenses (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0, ISC) are allowed without review.
Weak copyleft licenses (LGPL, MPL) are allowed for libraries used unmodified.
Strong copyleft licenses (GPL, AGPL) are not allowed in services or
libraries; the `license-check` CI job fails the build if one is detected.
Anything not in these lists needs Legal approval.

Production deploys start with a canary that receives 5% of traffic for ten

## Progressive rollout

After the canary, traffic shifts 25%, 50% and 100% at five-minute intervals.
Tier-1 services use ten-minute intervals. A deploy can be paused at any step
with `lark deploy pause <service>`.

## Rollback

Rollback redeploys the previous image tag; it does not revert code. Run
`lark deploy rollback <service>` or press "Rollback" on the deploy page in
Backstage. A rollback completes in under three minutes because the previous
image is still cached on every node. Rolling back does not undo database
migrations, which is why migrations must be backward compatible for at least
one release (see the database migrations page).

# Testing Strategy

Owner: Developer Experience (DevEx)

## The test pyramid

We aim for roughly 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests and 10% end-to-end
tests by count. Unit tests run on every commit, integration tests run on every
pull request, and end-to-end tests run on merge to `main` and nightly against
staging.

## Unit tests

Unit tests exercise one module in isolation and run without network, disk or
clock dependencies. A unit test suite for a service MUST finish in under 60
seconds on a laptop. Tests that need the clock use the injected `Clock`
interface; tests that need randomness seed it explicitly.

# Kubernetes Platform

Owner: Platform

## Clusters

Larkspur runs four Kubernetes clusters on managed cloud Kubernetes: `dev`,
`staging`, `prod-eu` and `prod-us`. Production clusters run three control
plane replicas across availability zones. Cluster versions track the upstream
release minus one minor version and are upgraded quarterly.

## Workload requirements

Every deployment MUST declare:

- CPU and memory requests and limits. Memory limit equals memory request;
  CPU limit is at most four times the CPU request.
- A readiness probe and a liveness probe on distinct endpoints
  (`/ready` and `/live`).
- A `PodDisruptionBudget` allowing at most one unavailable replica.
- Pod anti-affinity across zones for tier-1 services.
- Resource labels: `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `larkspur.com/team`,
  `larkspur.com/tier`.

The `kube-policy` admission controller rejects workloads missing any of
these.

Owner: Platform

## Layers

Larkspur caches at three layers, each with a different owner:

1. **Edge cache** - the CDN caches public, unauthenticated responses with

   and reference data. Owned by the service team.

## Monorepo versus polyrepo

Larkspur runs a hybrid model. Product services live in the `larkspur/platform`

monorepo unless the architecture review board grants an exception.

## Monorepo structure

```
platform/

  libs/<language>/<lib-name>/  # shared internal libraries
  tools/                       # build and developer tooling
  infra/                       # Kubernetes manifests and Helm values
  docs/                        # architecture decision records, runbooks
```

Each service directory contains a `service.yaml` manifest declaring the
owning team, the on-call rotation, the tier (1, 2 or 3) and the runtime.

## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by

someone reading the code later, or when the team debated it for more than an

consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by
the person making the decision, reviewed by the team.

Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, when it will surprise
someone reading the code later, or when the team debated it for more than an
hour. Choosing a library, deciding how to model a core entity, or picking a
consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

## What is an incident

An incident is any unplanned event that degrades a customer-facing service,
exposes data, or threatens to do either. When in doubt, declare: a false alarm
costs ten minutes; a late declaration costs hours.

## Severity levels

| Severity | Definition | Examples | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sev-1 | Total or major outage, data loss or security breach | checkout down for all customers | all hands, status page, executive update every 30 minutes |
| Sev-2 | Significant degradation for many customers | p95 latency 5x normal, one region down | incident channel, status page, update every hour |
| Sev-3 | Minor degradation or a workaround exists | one report type failing | owning team during business hours |
| Sev-4 | Cosmetic or internal-only | typo in an email | normal bug process |

Owner: Developer Experience (DevEx)

## Platform

CI runs on GitHub Actions with self-hosted runners in the `ci` Kubernetes
cluster. Runners are ephemeral: each job gets a fresh container and is
destroyed afterwards. The runner image is rebuilt weekly from

Every pull request runs these checks, and all must pass before merge:

- `lint` - formatters and linters in check mode
- `test` - unit tests with coverage upload

- `repo-lint` - required files, CODEOWNERS and naming rules

# Testing Strategy

Owner: Developer Experience (DevEx)

## The test pyramid

We aim for roughly 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests and 10% end-to-end
tests by count. Unit tests run on every commit, integration tests run on every
pull request, and end-to-end tests run on merge to `main` and nightly against
staging.

## Unit tests

Unit tests exercise one module in isolation and run without network, disk or
clock dependencies. A unit test suite for a service MUST finish in under 60
seconds on a laptop. Tests that need the clock use the injected `Clock`
interface; tests that need randomness seed it explicitly.

Caching > Cache-aside pattern
data. Services MUST function, albeit more slowly, when Redis is unavailable;
the client library returns a miss on connection errors and emits the
`cache_unavailable` metric.

## Stampede protection

Hot keys use a probabilistic early-expiry window and a per-key lock so that
only one request recomputes an expired value. The `larkspur-cache` library
implements this with `get_or_compute(key, ttl, fn)`.

## Invalidation

Caches are invalidated by publishing an event on the `cache.invalidate`
Kafka topic with the key pattern. Services subscribe and delete matching
keys. Time-based expiry remains the safety net; never rely on invalidation
alone for correctness-critical data.

# Backups and Disaster Recovery

Owner: Data Platform

## Backup schedule

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC
and ships write-ahead logs continuously to object storage in a different
region. Point-in-time recovery is possible to any second within the last 35
days. Object storage buckets that hold customer files are versioned and
replicated cross-region with a 15-minute lag.

## Restore testing

A random production database is restored into an isolated environment every
week by the `restore-drill` job. The drill verifies that the restore
completes, that row counts match the source within the expected lag, and
that the application's smoke tests pass against the restored copy. A failed
drill pages the Data Platform on-call.

Owner: Security and Legal

## Classification

Data is classified into four levels, and every datastore declares its highest
level in its `service.yaml`:

- **Public** - marketing content, published documentation.
- **Internal** - source code, runbooks, non-sensitive metrics.
- **Confidential** - customer business data, contracts, financial records.
- **Restricted** - personal data, payment card data, credentials.

## Retention periods

| Data | Retention | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Customer account data | life of the account plus 30 days | Product |
| Order and invoice records | 7 years (statutory) | Finance |
| Application logs | 30 days | SRE |
| Error logs | 1 year | SRE |
| Traces | 14 days | SRE |
| Analytics events | 13 months | Data |
| Backups | 35 days | Data Platform |
| Support tickets | 3 years | Support |

Retention is enforced by automated jobs, not by policy documents alone. A
datastore without an enforcement job cannot be promoted to production.

# Observability

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

## The three signals

Every service emits structured logs, Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry
traces. The `larkspur-telemetry` library for each language configures all
three with a single initialisation call and injects the `trace_id` into logs.

## Logging

Logs are JSON lines written to stdout and shipped by the cluster's Vector
agent to Loki. Required fields are `timestamp`, `level`, `service`,
`trace_id` and `message`. Log levels are `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN` and `ERROR`;
production runs at `INFO`. Logging request bodies or any personal data is
forbidden; the `log-scrubber` filter redacts known patterns (emails, card
numbers, bearer tokens) as a safety net, not as a substitute for care.

Log retention is 30 days in Loki, with `ERROR` lines additionally archived to
object storage for one year.

# Kubernetes Platform

Owner: Platform

## Clusters

Larkspur runs four Kubernetes clusters on managed cloud Kubernetes: `dev`,
`staging`, `prod-eu` and `prod-us`. Production clusters run three control
plane replicas across availability zones. Cluster versions track the upstream
release minus one minor version and are upgraded quarterly.

## Workload requirements

Every deployment MUST declare:

- CPU and memory requests and limits. Memory limit equals memory request;
  CPU limit is at most four times the CPU request.
- A readiness probe and a liveness probe on distinct endpoints
  (`/ready` and `/live`).
- A `PodDisruptionBudget` allowing at most one unavailable replica.
- Pod anti-affinity across zones for tier-1 services.
- Resource labels: `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `larkspur.com/team`,
  `larkspur.com/tier`.

The `kube-policy` admission controller rejects workloads missing any of
these.

## Forbidden operations in a single migration

- Adding a `NOT NULL` column without a default to a table with rows.
- Creating an index without `CONCURRENTLY` on a table over one million rows.
- Any statement that takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for more than two
  seconds on a tier-1 database.

The `migration-lint` check rejects the first three automatically.

## Why we use flags

Every user-visible change and every risky backend change ships behind a
feature flag. Flags decouple deploy from release: code reaches production
dark, is enabled for a small audience, and is expanded or rolled back without
a deploy.

Flags are managed in `flagship`, our internal flag service, and evaluated
through the `larkspur-flags` SDK available for Python, TypeScript and Go.
Evaluation is local: the SDK polls `flagship` every 30 seconds and caches the
ruleset, so a `flagship` outage leaves flags at their last known value.

# Caching

Owner: Platform

## Layers

Larkspur caches at three layers, each with a different owner:

1. **Edge cache** - the CDN caches public, unauthenticated responses with
   `Cache-Control` headers set by the service. Owned by Web Platform.
2. **Application cache** - Redis clusters, one per team, used for sessions,
   rate-limit counters and computed results. Owned by the service team.
3. **In-process cache** - small LRU caches inside a service for configuration
   and reference data. Owned by the service team.

Hot keys use a probabilistic early-expiry window and a per-key lock so that

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,

consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

# Backups and Disaster Recovery

Owner: Data Platform

## Backup schedule

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC
and ships write-ahead logs continuously to object storage in a different
region. Point-in-time recovery is possible to any second within the last 35
days. Object storage buckets that hold customer files are versioned and
replicated cross-region with a 15-minute lag.

## Restore testing

A random production database is restored into an isolated environment every
week by the `restore-drill` job. The drill verifies that the restore
completes, that row counts match the source within the expected lag, and
that the application's smoke tests pass against the restored copy. A failed
drill pages the Data Platform on-call.

Owner: Architecture Review Board

## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by
the person making the decision, reviewed by the team.

Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, when it will surprise
someone reading the code later, or when the team debated it for more than an
hour. Choosing a library, deciding how to model a core entity, or picking a
consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

# Database Migrations

Owner: Data Platform

## Tooling

Postgres schema changes are managed with `alembic` for Python services and
`goose` for Go services. Migration files are committed next to the service
and are reviewed like any other code, with the Data Platform team as a
required reviewer for tier-1 services.

## Backward compatibility

Every migration MUST be compatible with both the currently deployed version
and the version being deployed, because the deploy pipeline runs migrations
before the new code starts and a rollback does not undo migrations. In
practice this means the expand/contract pattern:

1. **Expand**: add the new column, table or index. Do not remove anything.
2. **Migrate**: deploy code that writes to both old and new shapes, then
   backfill.

We aim for roughly 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests and 10% end-to-end

# Backups and Disaster Recovery

Owner: Data Platform

## Backup schedule

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC
and ships write-ahead logs continuously to object storage in a different
region. Point-in-time recovery is possible to any second within the last 35
days. Object storage buckets that hold customer files are versioned and
replicated cross-region with a 15-minute lag.

## Restore testing

A random production database is restored into an isolated environment every
week by the `restore-drill` job. The drill verifies that the restore
completes, that row counts match the source within the expected lag, and
that the application's smoke tests pass against the restored copy. A failed
drill pages the Data Platform on-call.

## Backup schedule

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC

region. Point-in-time recovery is possible to any second within the last 35

replicated cross-region with a 15-minute lag.

A random production database is restored into an isolated environment every
week by the `restore-drill` job. The drill verifies that the restore
completes, that row counts match the source within the expected lag, and
that the application's smoke tests pass against the restored copy. A failed
drill pages the Data Platform on-call.

Owner: Data Platform

## Tooling

`goose` for Go services. Migration files are committed next to the service
and are reviewed like any other code, with the Data Platform team as a

Every migration MUST be compatible with both the currently deployed version
and the version being deployed, because the deploy pipeline runs migrations
before the new code starts and a rollback does not undo migrations. In
practice this means the expand/contract pattern:

1. **Expand**: add the new column, table or index. Do not remove anything.
2. **Migrate**: deploy code that writes to both old and new shapes, then
   backfill.

## Clusters

Larkspur runs four Kubernetes clusters on managed cloud Kubernetes: `dev`,
`staging`, `prod-eu` and `prod-us`. Production clusters run three control
plane replicas across availability zones. Cluster versions track the upstream
release minus one minor version and are upgraded quarterly.

  CPU limit is at most four times the CPU request.
- A readiness probe and a liveness probe on distinct endpoints
  (`/ready` and `/live`).

- Pod anti-affinity across zones for tier-1 services.
- Resource labels: `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `larkspur.com/team`,
  `larkspur.com/tier`.

The `kube-policy` admission controller rejects workloads missing any of
these.

# Architecture Decision Records

Owner: Architecture Review Board

## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by
the person making the decision, reviewed by the team.

## When to write one

Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, when it will surprise
someone reading the code later, or when the team debated it for more than an
hour. Choosing a library, deciding how to model a core entity, or picking a
consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

Hot keys use a probabilistic early-expiry window and a per-key lock so that

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,

consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

Owner: Architecture Review Board

## Purpose

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures a single technical decision,
its context and its consequences, so that future engineers understand why
the system looks the way it does. ADRs are lightweight: one page, written by
the person making the decision, reviewed by the team.

## When to write one

Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, when it will surprise
someone reading the code later, or when the team debated it for more than an
hour. Choosing a library, deciding how to model a core entity, or picking a
consistency model all qualify. Decisions that affect multiple teams need an
RFC instead.

Owner: Data Platform

## Backup schedule

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC
and ships write-ahead logs continuously to object storage in a different
region. Point-in-time recovery is possible to any second within the last 35
days. Object storage buckets that hold customer files are versioned and
replicated cross-region with a 15-minute lag.

## Restore testing

A random production database is restored into an isolated environment every
week by the `restore-drill` job. The drill verifies that the restore
completes, that row counts match the source within the expected lag, and
that the application's smoke tests pass against the restored copy. A failed
drill pages the Data Platform on-call.

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC

Every production Postgres cluster takes a full base backup daily at 02:00 UTC

Production deploys start with a canary that receives 5% of traffic for ten

posts to the owning team's alerts channel.

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

## Why tiers exist

Not every service needs the same rigour. Tiers let us apply the strictest
requirements (two reviewers, load tests, canary analysis, 99.95%

## Tier definitions

- **Tier 1**: an outage stops customers from buying, paying or using a core
  workflow, or exposes data. Examples: `api-gateway`, `order-router`,
  `payments-ledger`, `identity`.

Every user-visible change and every risky backend change ships behind a

## Clusters

Larkspur runs four Kubernetes clusters on managed cloud Kubernetes: `dev`,

## Layers

Larkspur caches at three layers, each with a different owner:

1. **Edge cache** - the CDN caches public, unauthenticated responses with
   `Cache-Control` headers set by the service. Owned by Web Platform.

   rate-limit counters and computed results. Owned by the service team.
3. **In-process cache** - small LRU caches inside a service for configuration
   and reference data. Owned by the service team.
